t: LeetCode 3143 — Maximum Points Inside the Square
o: A square centered at the origin with edges parallel to the axes contains exactly those points whose Chebyshev distance $r_i = \max(|x_i|, |y_i|)$ is at most half its side length. So each point has a single scalar "radius", and choosing a square is equivalent to choosing a threshold $R$: we take every point with $r_i \le R$, provided no tag appears twice among them. In Example 1 the radii are 2, 2, 4, 3, 3 for tags a,b,d,c,a — taking everything up to radius 2 gives {a,b} = 2 points; going further would grab both c-points first (fine), but eventually both a-points, which is invalid. In Example 2, tag 'b' occurs twice with radii 2 and 2, so the threshold must stay below 2, leaving only the single 'a' point. With n up to 1e5 we need roughly linear time after a sort.
k: A point lies inside an origin-centered axis-aligned square iff max(|x|,|y|) ≤ R, so the problem reduces to picking a radius threshold.
If we add points in increasing order of radius, validity is easy to maintain: the moment a tag would repeat, we must stop entirely.
Equivalently, for each tag compute its two smallest radii; the threshold cannot reach the second-smallest radius of any tag.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort by Radius + Greedy Sweep
a.i: Sort all points by Chebyshev radius. Scan them in increasing radius, keeping a set of tags already taken. Every point encountered before the first repeated tag can be safely included, because including a point never forces us to include anything with a larger radius. The first time we meet a tag that is already in the set, we cannot take this point, and since all remaining points have radius ≥ this one, none of them can be added either — so the answer is the count accumulated so far. If we finish the scan with no conflict, the answer is n.
s: Compute r_i = max(|x_i|, |y_i|) for every point.
Sweep in increasing radius with a boolean array seen[26] of tags.
If s[i] was already seen, return the current count; otherwise mark the tag and increment count.
Return count (= n) if the sweep completes without conflict.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting by radius dominates; the sweep itself is O(n).
a.sp: O(n) for the index array (plus O(1) for the tag set); O(1) extra if sorting points in place.

a.n: Approach 2: Per-Tag Two Smallest Radii (No Sorting)
a.i: For each tag, only its two smallest radii matter: if a tag appears twice, the square's threshold must stay strictly below the smaller of those two values (otherwise both copies enter). Let limit be the minimum over all tags of their second-smallest radius (infinity if every tag is unique). Then the answer is simply the number of points whose radius is strictly less than limit — these are exactly the points any valid maximal square can contain, and they are automatically conflict-free because every conflicting pair has its larger member at radius ≥ limit. This avoids sorting entirely with a single pass using fixed-size arrays.
s: Keep arrays min1[26], min2[26] initialized to infinity; also track the overall minimum radius.
For each point compute r = max(|x|, |y|); update min1/min2 for its tag.
Set limit = min over tags of min2[tag] (tags appearing once contribute infinity).
Count points with r < limit and return that count.
a.t: O(n) — two linear passes with constant-size auxiliary arrays; coordinates fit in 32 bits but use 64-bit radii to be safe against overflow in intermediates.
a.sp: O(1) — only two fixed-size arrays of length 26 beyond the input.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1 (sort + greedy): it directly matches the mental model of growing the square and is easy to justify. Then mention Approach 2 as the O(n) refinement once you notice only the two smallest radii per tag matter. Pitfalls: using Euclidean or Manhattan distance instead of Chebyshev max(|x|,|y|); forgetting that points on the boundary count as inside (so the threshold must be strict relative to a duplicated tag's second-smallest radius, while equal-radius distinct tags are fine); integer overflow when squaring coordinates in other formulations. Edge cases: all unique tags (answer n), a tag repeated at the very smallest radius (answer may be 0 as in Example 3), and n = 1 (answer 1). Follow-ups might ask to reconstruct the actual square side length (it is 2 × the largest included radius) or to handle multiple squares / weighted points.
